title: Division Algorithm
body:
For any integer $a$ and positive integer $d$, there are unique integers $q$ (quotient) and
$r$ (remainder) with

$$a = qd + r, \qquad 0 \le r < d$$

That is the whole statement, and the two operators in C++ hand you the two halves:

```c++
int a = 17, d = 5;
int q = a / d;    // 3   the quotient
int r = a % d;    // 2   the remainder
// 17 == 3 * 5 + 2
```

`a / d` on two [[Integer]]s truncates rather than rounding. `17 / 5` is `3`, and `18 / 5` is
also `3`. Nothing rounds up, ever. If you want a real answer, one operand has to be a
[[Double]]: see [[Type casting]].

The remainder is the useful half:

| Question | Expression |
|---|---|
| Does `d` divide `n`? | `n % d == 0` |
| Is `n` even? | `n % 2 == 0` |
| Last digit of `n` | `n % 10` |
| Strip the last digit | `n / 10` |
| Wrap an index into `0..size-1` | `i % size` |

The last-digit pair is the loop that reverses a number, sums its digits, or converts it to
another base, and it terminates because `n / 10` reaches 0. That is the standard
[[While loop]] exercise.

Warning on negatives: C++ truncates toward zero, so `-17 / 5` is `-3` and `-17 % 5` is `-2`.
The mathematical division algorithm above insists $r \ge 0$, which would give $q = -4$,
$r = 3$. The language and the theorem disagree on negative inputs, and it is the language you
have to live with. [[DISCRETE MATH]] uses the theorem's version, and modular arithmetic in
[[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] depends on it.

Built on top of this: [[GCD and LCM]] via the Euclidean algorithm, and [[Prime Number]]
testing by trial division.

One rung further up, [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) stops treating the remainder as a value and
makes it an object: the congruence class. That is [[Modular Arithmetic]], and it turns this
theorem into the construction of $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
